column4: Noah's water itself “طَغَا ٱلْمَاءُ,” giving the section's moral excess its exact physical source-scene: water rises past its bound, while the ark carries those spared from it.
Thamud are destroyed “بِٱلطَّاغِيَةِ”; the same root names both their excess in the section and the overwhelming thing by which that excess returns upon them.
The human being wants “لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ,” an exact moral use of the section's bursting root: the impulse seeks an open course ahead with no restraining bank.
God dislikes the hypocrites' “ٱنۢبِعَاثَهُمْ” and holds them back; it is the section's same launching motion, here checked before a harmful group can set out.

This explains why the mobilization in 9:46 is checked: had they gone out, they would have rushed among the believers seeking discord, the social counterpart of one impulse making a group flow after it.
The declaration that the human being “لَيَطْغَىٰ” directly generalizes Thamud's boundary-crossing from a people to the human tendency within the self.
It locates the breach behind 96:6 in seeing oneself self-sufficient; imagined independence removes the felt need for a limit.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh because “إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ,” the same diagnosis of moral overflow applied to another ruler who has crossed the limit.
Moses offers the overflowing Pharaoh purification—“أَن تَزَكَّىٰ”—placing growth by cleansing directly opposite growth by excess.
“فَأَمَّا مَن طَغَىٰ” opens the general reckoning for whoever crosses the bound, extending Thamud's choice beyond its historical scene.
Preferring the nearer life specifies what feeds the transgression named in 79:37.
Hell as the transgressor's refuge completes the returning consequence begun in 79:37: the outward destination answers the inward breach.
Fear of standing before the Lord and forbidding the self its desire is the section's dam stated as an act: the soul is actively held back.
The Garden as refuge completes the result of the self-restraint in 79:40, opposite the transgressor's refuge in 79:39.
Salih's “فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ” addresses Thamud with the protective alternative to the excess that carries them away.
“Do not obey the command of the extravagant” is the social dam: Salih tries to stop the people from flowing behind boundary-crossing leaders.
The leaders forbidden in 26:151 spread corruption and do not set things right, identifying the direction in which their unchecked command carries the group.
The prohibition against harming the she-camel draws the concrete line Thamud must not cross and warns that punishment will seize them if they do.
They hamstring the camel and then become remorseful; collective agency follows the forbidden act and recognition comes only after the barrier has failed.
“The punishment seized them” completes the section's reversal: what rushed outward from them returns as the force that overtakes them.
The ruined peoples are those who “طَغَوْا۟ فِى ٱلْبِلَادِ,” turning a crossed inward bound into excess spread across whole lands.
They multiplied corruption there; this is the outward proliferation produced by the transgression named in 89:11.
God “poured” a scourge of punishment upon them, giving the consequence the section's downward, fluid counter-motion to their rising excess.
Thamud call their companion, and he takes up the act and hamstrings the camel; this is the clearest other staging of one culprit acting as the people's summoned agent.
The warning and punishment immediately answer the companion's act in 54:29, joining the single initiative to the collective consequence.
The single blast leaves the people like an enclosure-builder's dry brushwood, giving concrete form to the collective devastation announced in 54:30.
The water is apportioned between Thamud and the camel, a measured boundary around water that the people are required to honor rather than overrun.
Thamud hamstring the camel, disdain their Lord's command, and challenge the threatened punishment; the act is explicitly framed as crossing a commanded bound.
The earthquake then seizes the community in its homes, another exact form of the transgressing act returning as an overwhelming seizure.
Nine bands in Salih's city corrupt the land and do not reform it; the single worst actor belongs to an organized current of instigators.
God points to the outcome of their plot: the plotters and their people are destroyed together, joining instigation to communal consequence.
In the same Salih account, believers who practiced taqwa are saved; the protective course produces the opposite outcome from the corrupters' surge.
Thamud prefer blindness over guidance, restaging the section's inward choice before the thunderbolt takes them.
Those who believed and practiced taqwa are rescued from the same event, so taqwa functions as the separating protection within Thamud's disaster.
Thamud insolently defy their Lord's command and the thunderbolt seizes them while they watch, making the violated limit and its returning force contiguous.
They cannot rise or defend themselves after the seizure, reversing the forceful rising of the section's “ٱنۢبَعَثَ.”
The ayah directly opposes the God-conscious to “ٱلْفُجَّارِ,” matching the two contrary capacities—fujur and taqwa—placed within the soul.
God increases the guided in guidance and “gives them their taqwa,” a close parallel to the section's soul being given awareness of its protective capacity.
Whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul prospers; the feared force is internal and protection is placed between the self and its own impulse.
The repeated promise that one protected from the soul's avarice prospers states the section's dam in literal root language and links it to success.
“Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire” makes the root's dictionary picture explicit: persons must place protection between themselves and what is feared.
Two bodies of water are released to meet, furnishing the section's literal scene of powerful currents set in motion.
A barrier stands between those waters so they do not overrun it; surge, intervening barrier, and observed limit are all present in one scene.
A people ask for a barrier against Gog and Magog because they spread corruption in the land, turning restraint of social فساد into a literal dam.
Dhu al-Qarnayn offers to make a rampart “between you and them,” exactly enacting the section's definition of protection by placing something between two sides.
The completed barrier cannot be scaled or pierced, showing what an intact protective limit does against a force seeking passage.
The gates of heaven are opened with pouring water, beginning the outer flood that answers the people's persistent rejection.
The earth is made to burst with springs—“وَفَجَّرْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا”—and the waters meet by a measured decree, joining rupture, flood, and measure.
Noah's son seeks a mountain as protection from the water, but no protector exists that day and a wave comes between them; a presumed barrier fails before the flood.
The flood takes Noah's people while they are wrongdoers; wrongdoing and an outward torrent that overtakes its agents coincide without metaphorical reconstruction.
Because of their sins Noah's people are drowned and then entered into Fire; the punishment arrives through the water after the moral breach.
In the same flood context, Noah calls the future offspring “فَاجِرًا كَفَّارًا,” placing the moral f-j-r term beside the deluge caused by entrenched wrongdoing.
At sea, waves surround the travelers and they call on God sincerely; the literal overwhelming water supplies the setting for the moral turn in the next ayah.
Once rescued, they commit excess on earth, and are told that their excess is only against themselves; the flood-survivor's transgression is explicitly made self-returning.
Pharaoh and his armies pursue Israel through the sea in aggression and excess until drowning overtakes him, joining moral overreach to the water that finally takes its agent.
Pharaoh follows Moses with his troops and the sea overwhelms them, combining a leader, a following group, and the returning flood that takes the transgressor.
Pharaoh is said to have led his people astray rather than guided them, naming the collective direction imposed by the overflowing leader in 20:78.
God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea; the paradigmatic transgressor and those mobilized with him are taken by water together.
When Pharaoh's people provoke divine retribution, all of them are drowned; their ruler's elevated excess returns as collective inundation.
Twelve springs burst from the struck stone, yet each group knows its drinking place; the same physical bursting is beneficial when apportioned and bounded.
The seas are “فُجِّرَتْ,” the root's physical bursting on a cosmic scale and the most direct counterpart to the section's water-image.
In the same surah that depicts seas bursting, “ٱلْفُجَّارَ” are destined for Hell; the root's physical and moral registers reproduce the section's central meeting.
Cooperation in righteousness and taqwa is set against cooperation in sin and aggression, showing that groups can reinforce either the dam or the surge.
Disobedience and repeated transgression bring a communal curse, supplying the collective setting for the failure of restraint stated next.
They did not forbid one another the wrong they did; the missing social barrier lets wrongdoing pass from individual act into communal condition.
Believers are told to guard against a trial that will not strike only the wrongdoers among them, a precise warning that one group's breach can become an engulfing consequence.
Earlier communities lacked enough people who forbade corruption on earth; those few who did are described as saved, making social restraint the alternative to collective destruction.
God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reforming, completing the protective effect of the restraint described in 11:116.
A people's outer condition changes with what they change within themselves; when evil is decreed there is no repeller, closely matching the section's inward breach becoming outward disaster.
Israel is warned not to transgress within good provision lest wrath descend and whoever incurs it fall, pairing a stated limit with the consequence of crossing it.
“Do not transgress in the balance” gives tughyan a measured boundary: excess is precisely movement past a just proportion.
Maintaining weight with justice states positively the measure that prevents the transgression prohibited in 55:8.
Giving and practicing taqwa begin one of two opposed human courses, echoing the paired capacities placed in the soul.
Affirming the finest truth supplies the orientation joined to taqwa in 92:5.
God eases the person of taqwa toward ease, the outward course corresponding to the inward protective choice.
The opposite course begins with withholding and imagining oneself self-sufficient, the same condition named as the cause of human tughyan in 96:7.
Denial accompanies that self-sufficiency, paralleling Thamud's denial through its excess.
God eases the self-sufficient denier toward hardship, completing the opposed outcome of the two inward courses.
Leaders deny having coercive authority over their followers and say the followers themselves were a transgressing people; this sharpens responsibility within a group that flows after instigators.
The leaders admit leading others astray while also being astray, showing transmission of direction without erasing the followers' own choice.
People in the Fire confess that obeying leaders and great men led them away from the path, a direct after-scene of collective obedience to human instigators.
They ask for doubled punishment on those leaders, exposing how the followed impulse returns as conflict over shared responsibility.
The Prophet is told not to obey one who follows desire and whose affair has gone beyond bounds; refusal of obedience becomes a barrier against another person's unchecked impulse.
The soul is described as persistently commanding evil unless the Lord has mercy, identifying the inward pressure that the section's protective barrier must check.
When Gog and Magog are released, they stream down from every elevation; the people formerly held behind the rampart become a human flood once the barrier opens.
God seizes Pharaoh with the punishment of his latter and former acts, completing the consequence of the tughyan diagnosed in 79:17.
Pharaoh's end is called a lesson for one who fears, matching the fearful stance that enables restraint in 79:40.
The earlier commission to Moses repeats the diagnosis “إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ,” confirming boundary-crossing as the reason the messenger confronts Pharaoh.
Moses and Aaron together are sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, adding the paired messengers' effort to check the ruler's excess.
The righteous make a spring “يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا”; the same bursting root becomes a directed, life-giving flow rather than moral rupture or destructive inundation.
God causes a river to burst through two fruitful gardens; physical f-j-r here sustains ordered abundance, showing that direction and bounds determine the force's value.
Springs are made to gush among gardens so people may eat their fruit, a productive counterpart to the section's destructive burst.
Fresh and salt waters are released together but a barrier and forbidding partition remain between them; strong currents coexist without violating their appointed distinction.
A barrier placed between two seas is named among signs of divine ordering, the physical counterpart of a protective limit established between forces.
A wall with a gate separates believers from hypocrites, with mercy inside and punishment outside; the barrier makes protection and exposure visibly opposite sides.
The person trying to shield the face from punishment has no adequate barrier; it reverses taqwa's preventive protection by showing protection attempted only after consequence arrives.
The Prophet's sight neither swerves nor “طَغَىٰ”; the same root marks a boundary successfully observed rather than morally crossed.
Some stones split and water emerges, while human hearts remain harder; the physical fissure releases life, whereas inward hardness refuses the opening toward guidance.
God leaves hypocrites wandering blindly in their tughyan; the ayah presents unchecked excess as a condition in which direction itself is lost.
Revelation increases many opponents in transgression and unbelief, showing a refused check becoming fuel for further overflow and conflict.
The message sent down increases many People of the Book in transgression and unbelief; like Pharaoh's refused invitation, offered guidance can expose a deeper breach.
After the first refusal to believe, hearts and eyes are turned and people are left wandering in transgression; an initial breach becomes a sustained course.
Those left without guidance wander in their tughyan, giving the section's rushing motion the added feature of directionless movement.
People who do not expect the meeting with God are left blindly wandering in tughyan while punishment is delayed; the unblocked course continues before consequence arrives.
Warnings and signs increase the wrongdoers only in great tughyan, another instance in which a proposed limit is converted into further excess.
Moses and Aaron fear that Pharaoh may act precipitately against them or transgress; the root here names the ruler's threatened movement beyond restraint.
Even mercy and removal of affliction would leave these people obstinately persisting in tughyan, portraying excess as a current they refuse to leave.
The evil companion denies having made the human transgress and says he was already far astray; this qualifies the image of followers by preserving personal agency.
The rejecters' accusations are traced either to their reason or to their being a transgressing people, linking denial of a messenger to tughyan as in Thamud's denial.
After their garden is ruined, its owners confess “إِنَّا كُنَّا طَاغِينَ”; consequence makes them recognize the boundary-crossing that preceded it.
Hell is described as a destination for the transgressors, concisely stating the end toward which unchecked tughyan runs.
The transgressors are assigned an evil return, making return itself the frame for their consequence.
Hell, which they enter, specifies the evil return announced for the transgressors in 38:55.
After the poured scourge, the Lord is said to be at the watchpost; excess never escapes the boundary of divine observation and answer.
The people of taqwa restrain anger and pardon others, a concrete human act in which an inward surge is held rather than discharged.
When a satanic impulse touches those with taqwa, remembrance restores clear sight; taqwa interrupts an incipient motion before it becomes action.
God delivers those who practiced taqwa to their place of safety and no evil touches them, showing the completed protective result of the inner barrier.
The angels ask God to protect believers from evil deeds and say that one protected that Day receives mercy; the root's shielding force is made explicit.
Amid the opponents' heated zeal, God binds the believers to the word of taqwa; imposed steadiness checks a contagious group passion.
Fasting is prescribed so that believers may attain taqwa, presenting disciplined restraint as a means of forming the soul's protective capacity.
A calamity that strikes is tied to what people's hands have earned, stating plainly the section's movement from inward deed to outward blow.
Corruption appears on land and sea because of human deeds so that people taste part of what they did; the damaged world returns human action to its makers.
God does not change a favor until a people change what is within themselves, another explicit hinge between inward alteration and collective outward reversal.
Destroyed peoples wrong themselves, and the powers they invoke only add to their ruin; the consequence is traced back into their own act.
The one who purifies himself prospers, affirming the growth offered to Pharaoh in 79:18 as the opposite course to tughyan.

Moses' companion fears that the boy would burden believing parents with tughyan and unbelief; this may extend the water-image relationally, as one person's excess threatens to overwhelm others, but the exact force of the verb is debated.
